152d01eb38b59792.en:
Let me check the latest on Iran. 

The war's in day two hundred thirty-eight. It started February twenty-eighth with joint US-Israeli strikes Trump called major combat operations. Khamenei was killed in those early strikes — his son Mojtaba took over. There was a June memorandum of understanding to wind it down, Trump tore it up in July, and since then it's been a naval blockade, sporadic exchanges, and a lot of posturing.

Right now the US role is basically three things. One, holding the blockade and claiming control of the Strait of Hormuz — Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it's closed, CENTCOM says it's open for business, and tankers keep getting hit by mines either way. Two, preparing to escalate after the November third midterms. Trump's said flat-out he won't strike before then, but the Pentagon's drawn up options including the mother of all bomb on Pickaxe Mountain, the deep underground nuclear site. Hegseth flew to Israel unannounced this week to meet Netanyahu, who told Trump they have a job to finish. Three, the economic squeeze — oil's over a hundred a barrel, Brent around one-oh-eight, and Trump's betting Iran's economy collapses before anything else has to.

The honest read? Trump's framing swings between "we could leave right now, they're finished" and "we'll finish the job soon" — sometimes in the same week. Iran's negotiating position hasn't budged despite the damage. Western intelligence still thinks Iran can replenish missiles and drones. So the gap between the victory narrative and the reality on the ground is where the risk lives. A three-day post-election campaign sounds clean on paper, but you can't control how Iran answers.

One wrinkle worth watching: Russia's foreign minister Lavrov just made his first visit to Tehran since the war began, and Iran's foreign minister says ties with Moscow have never been closer. Trump's claiming Russia's doing almost nothing to help — that contradiction is probably not an accident.

Want me to dig into any piece of that — the Hormuz economics, the post-midterm strike options, or what Lavrov's visit actually signals?

Mostly politics. A strike that sends oil past a hundred-twenty or gets US troops killed in the final stretch would hand Democrats a gift two weeks before voters go to the polls. He's already said it outright — the war ends right after November third. There's also Israel's election on October twenty-seventh, and he's endorsed Netanyahu, so the sequencing serves both campaigns. The cynical version is that he's optimizing for Republican seats, not for Iran policy. The slightly less cynical version is that he genuinely believes a post-election shock will force capitulation before a new Congress can constrain him. Either way, the calendar is doing more strategic work than the bombs are right now.

The part that should make people nervous is that "we won't strike before the election" is a promise with a built-in expiration date, not a principle.

6bff2258d700c691.en:
He probably does think it'll turn out differently, and the belief has a name — the **edge theory**. One adviser told the Atlantic that economic pressure is working and Iran is close to the edge, so a few more strikes would push them over. That's the whole bet: not that bombing destroys the regime, but that it arrives at the exact moment the economy breaks and the population turns. The problem is every intelligence assessment says Iran's negotiating position hasn't moved despite eight months of this. So either Trump knows something the analysts don't, or he's running the same experiment and expecting a different result. Given his track record with predictions — the war would take weeks back in March — I'd put more weight on the second one.

What's interesting is the alternative he won't say out loud: that this was never really about forcing surrender, it's about not being the

Un asesor le dijo a The Atlantic que la presión económica está funcionando y que Irán está cerca del borde, así que unos cuantos ataques más lo empujarían al otro lado. Esa es toda la apuesta: no que los bombardeos destruyan el régimen, sino que lleguen justo en el momento en que la economía se rompe y la población se vuelve. El problema es que todas las evaluaciones de inteligencia dicen que la posición negociadora de Irán no se ha movido pese a ocho meses de esto. Así que o Trump sabe algo que los analistas no saben, o está repitiendo el mismo experimento y espera un resultado distinto. Visto su historial con las predicciones —la guerra iba a durar semanas, allá por marzo—, yo le daría más peso a lo segundo.

Lo interesante es la alternativa que no va a decir en voz alta: que esto nunca fue realmente de forzar una rendición, sino de no ser el

87fb6d98dc46a49f.en:
Searching for how the Starshield restoration unfolded. 

The reversal started Wednesday. Trump called Musk directly and told him he was frustrated the speeds were still capped around a hundred miles an hour. He'd apparently been telling aides and close associates all week he wanted it reversed. By Thursday, US and Ukrainian officials said the system was working more normally — though not fully. Some units reported higher speeds, others still saw constant interruptions.

Then came the public messaging mess. On Thursday Trump wouldn't confirm the call at all. "Whether I called or whether somebody else called, doesn't make any difference. The bottom line — he put it back." On Friday he flipped and said he hadn't spoken to Musk and might have to if it's not fixed. When CNN pressed him on who ordered the slowdown in the first place, he said, "I have no idea, but I wouldn't tell you if I did."

Meanwhile the rest of the administration scattered in different directions. Rubio insisted it was purely SpaceX's call, not the White House. Hegseth said the Pentagon never directed anything. Vance hinted there had been coordination. Senator Cornyn said he didn't believe Musk would have acted without at least White House acquiescence. And Senator Blumenthal opened a formal inquiry into who had the authority to degrade a system the Pentagon had spent billions on.

The political logic of the reversal is pretty clear. The slowdown was generating bad headlines at the worst possible time — civilian casualties in Ukraine surging, European allies alarmed, a Democratic senator investigating, and Trump trying to sell voters a story about strength on Iran and energy prices. Keeping the cap on wasn't worth the cost. But reversing it publicly would mean admitting the original move was a mistake, or worse, that it was deliberate coercion. So Trump split the difference: get it fixed quietly, claim credit obliquely, deny the call, and leave everyone arguing about whose fault it was.

The deeper issue it exposed is that a private company now holds a switch that can alter a war's outcome overnight, and nobody in government has a clean answer for who controls it. That's the part that doesn't go away even if the speeds come back.

One thing worth watching: if Ukraine starts seriously shopping for European satellite alternatives, this stops being a one-off and becomes a structural shift in who Kyiv depends on. I could dig into what those alternatives actually look like if you want.

La ralentización estaba generando malos titulares en el peor momento posible: las bajas civiles en Ucrania se disparaban, los aliados europeos estaban alarmados, un senador demócrata investigaba y Trump intentaba vender a los votantes un relato de fortaleza sobre Irán y los precios de la energía. Esa es la parte que no se va aunque vuelvan las velocidades.

db39f21342b97906.en:
Taking that further. Starshield runs on Pentagon money but under SpaceX's terms of service. The whitelist that locked Russia out was a joint SpaceX-and-Ukrainian-defense-ministry invention — not a military order, a commercial agreement. So when Musk throttled it, he wasn't disobeying anyone. He was exercising rights he arguably had under the contract. That's the trap: the government outsourced a war-critical function and forgot to write the clause that says "and we can take it back."

Musk's own framing makes it worse. He told an X user that Starshield is under US government control and that the government made the call — then separately said limits are decided by the US military and ultimately the president. Both things can't be true unless the real answer is that nobody knows, and both men are comfortable letting the ambiguity stand because it protects each of them. Trump gets deniability. Musk gets to look like he was following orders without admitting he took any.

The precedent is the scary part. If this works once — throttle a private system, reverse it when the politics sour, never resolve who ordered it — it becomes the template. Next time it's Taiwan, and the question isn't whether SpaceX will comply. It's whether the owner agrees with the mission.

Blumenthal's letter is the right first move, but it's congressional oversight after the fact. What actually fixes this is legislation defining when a commercial satellite network becomes a strategic asset with mandatory government access — like the Communications Act did for undersea cables a century ago. Nobody's drafted that yet because writing it means admitting how dependent the military already is.

I could pull the actual contract language between SpaceX and the Pentagon on Starshield to see exactly what override rights exist — or don't.
db39f21342b97906.tr:
Llevándolo más lejos. Starshield funciona con dinero del Pentágono, pero bajo los términos de servicio de SpaceX. La lista blanca que dejó fuera a Rusia fue un invento conjunto de SpaceX y el ministerio de Defensa ucraniano: no una orden militar, un acuerdo comercial. Así que, cuando Musk lo limitó, no estaba desobedeciendo a nadie. Estaba ejerciendo derechos que, se puede argumentar, tenía según el contrato. Esa es la trampa: el gobierno externalizó una función crítica para la guerra y se olvidó de escribir la cláusula que dice «y podemos recuperarlo».

La propia forma en que Musk lo plantea lo empeora. Le dijo a un usuario de X que Starshield está bajo control del gobierno de EE. UU. y que el gobierno tomó la decisión; y luego, por separado, dijo que los límites los decide el ejército estadounidense y, en última instancia, el presidente. Las dos cosas no pueden ser ciertas a menos que la respuesta real sea que nadie lo sabe, y que ambos se sienten cómodos dejando la ambigüedad en pie porque protege a cada uno. Trump se queda con la negación plausible. Musk queda como si hubiera seguido órdenes sin admitir que tomó ninguna.

El precedente es la parte que da miedo. Si esto funciona una vez —limitar un sistema privado, revertirlo cuando la política se pone fea, no resolver nunca quién lo ordenó—, se convierte en la plantilla. La próxima vez es Taiwán, y la pregunta no es si SpaceX va a cumplir. Es si el dueño está de acuerdo con la misión.

La carta de Blumenthal es el primer paso correcto, pero es supervisión del Congreso a posteriori. Lo que de verdad arregla esto es una ley que defina cuándo una red comercial de satélites se convierte en un activo estratégico con acceso obligatorio del gobierno, como hizo la Communications Act con los cables submarinos hace un siglo. Nadie ha redactado eso todavía porque escribirlo significa admitir lo dependiente que ya es el ejército.

Podría sacar la redacción real del contrato entre SpaceX y el Pentágono sobre Starshield para ver exactamente qué derechos de anulación existen… o no.

The Pentagon's whole case against Anthropic was that Claude's built-in restrictions could deny, disrupt, or manipulate military operations — which is exactly what Musk just did with Starshield, in real time, with real drones falling out of the sky. The D.C. Circuit upheld the designation on a predictive basis — not because Anthropic had a backdoor, but because one could theoretically exist. That's the double standard in one image: a company that refuses to hand over unrestricted AI gets blacklisted as a national security threat, while the company that actually restricted a military system gets a courtesy call and a press statement. Anthropic's still fighting — they asked for a rehearing in mid-October, and seventeen former national security officials filed a brief this week warning the ruling threatens every defense contractor. Déjame ver qué ha dicho últimamente.

Sacks no ha publicado nada directamente sobre el tope de velocidad de Starshield. Pero su patrón está bastante claro. En 2023, cuando estalló la historia de Crimea, publicó que ninguna buena acción queda sin castigo: Musk ofreció Starlink gratis, Ucrania le pidió en una llamada a altas horas de la noche que habilitara un ataque provocador contra la flota rusa, él se negó porque temía una escalada, y los medios lo llamaron traidor. La lectura de Sacks entonces fue que el dueño de una empresa privada tiene derecho a decidir cómo se usa su tecnología, y que los neocons necesitaban un chivo expiatorio cuando fracasó su contraofensiva.

Probablemente acabaría en el mismo sitio ahora. Musk es dueño del hardware, los términos de Starshield nunca se redactaron bien como para darle al Pentágono un poder de anulación, y el verdadero escándalo no es que Musk accionara una palanca, sino que el gobierno gastara miles de millones dependiendo de un interruptor que no controlaba. También señalaría el contraste con Anthropic: la empresa que entrenó a Claude para que potencialmente se negara a cumplir órdenes, como objetor de conciencia, recibe una designación de seguridad nacional, mientras que el tipo que de verdad restringió un sistema militar en activo recibe una llamada y un encogimiento de hombros. Sacks diría que eso es aplicación selectiva disfrazada de política de seguridad.

El único punto en el que podría dudar es el ángulo del diésel a cambio de silencio. Sacks ha sido de línea dura con Rusia en el pasado, y si el tope de velocidad fue realmente para proteger el acuerdo de combustible de Trump con Putin, eso le resulta más difícil de vender como que Musk se plantó frente al blob. Probablemente lo reformularía como que a Musk lo usaron de válvula de alivio, lo cual, para ser justos, no está tan lejos de lo que realmente pasó.
